records.inputs: A published paper or theory specification, an xAct/Mathematica environment, the curated entry corpus and the shell toolkit with its persistent kernel, method and trap notes
records.outputs: Replayable machine-verifiable entries (record plus inputs-only evaluation notebook), fresh-kernel verification transcripts, session and progress logs, and a stall report when the ladder is triggered
records.notes: Single-author Wolfram Language paclet (Vasil Dimitrov, INRNE, Bulgarian Academy of Sciences) built on xAct that stores a supergravity theory or solution as code which replays in a fresh kernel and carries its own verification. Code is AGPL-3.0-or-later (versions up to 2.0.0 were MIT) and the bundled corpora are CC BY 4.0; version 2.1.0 is on GitHub and in the Wolfram Paclet Repository, but the agent toolkit ships only with the GitHub repository. The experimental agent/ toolkit, for shell-capable agents on macOS or Linux, gives an external coding agent a persistent kernel with enforced time budgets and restart-and-replay recovery, a reporter that re-runs a script on a fresh kernel, symptom-keyed method and trap notes, and an advisory stall ladder that tells the agent when to stop and write a report. In three reported runs driven through Claude Code, the agent built 3d Einstein-AdS gravity and the BTZ solution from scratch, then recreated two sections of a published paper on accelerating AdS4 black holes; runs 1 and 2 together took under three hours, and the five authored entries, each replayed on a fresh kernel, are published under Data/Vasko-bot/. The human gave three task prompts and two interruptions, one of them a coordinate-change hint the paper credits with the largest speed-up, and runs the resulting notebook. Limits: the package itself is computer-algebra infrastructure, the model behind the runs is not stated, Claude Code also wrote the toolkit and most of the paper's agent section, and run journals and resource ledgers are available only on request.

records.name: SPARC (scanning probe agentic research cycle)
aliases: Human-agent discovery of reconfigurable in-plane ferroelectric superdomain control
records.domain: Agentic scanning-probe microscopy of ferroelectric superdomain control
records.inputs: A campaign target, piezoresponse microscopy data, instrument-control tools, and the persistent FINDINGS.md and PITFALLS.md memory files with their compiled preflight checks
records.outputs: Agent-designed pulse-lattice write programs executed on the microscope, graded findings and failure records, per-iteration measurements, and reconfigured in-plane superdomain patterns
records.notes: University of Tennessee and Rice team (Liu, Slautin, Lin, Kim, Martin, Kalinin) pairing a coding agent, Claude Opus 4.1 in Claude Code on the instrument computer, with one piezoresponse microscope, one shared notebook, and two persistent memory files: FINDINGS.md for graded conclusions and PITFALLS.md for learned failure modes, with selected pitfalls compiled into checks that refuse a design before any voltage reaches the tip. In the operator-controlled Campaign 1 the agent built the state variable, hypotheses and write programs while the operator executed every write. In the agent-controlled Campaign 2 the agent issued instrument commands through a Python wrapper, closed nine propose-preflight-write-read-analyze-decide cycles, self-halted eight of them, rejected two of its own provisional rules by direct measurement, and wrote a mask-defined UTK pattern (letters about 3 µm across) into the measured in-plane superdomain response of a PbZr0.2Ti0.8O3(111) film. Disclosed gates in Campaign 2: the operator supplied the target, stayed present with stop authority, sent 117 prompts over three instrument days, and moved the stage to fresh areas between sessions; an exclusive instrument lock, a file-level stop command and limits on scanner range, bias, footprint and write budget bounded candidate writes. The authors report that six of eight launches failed on faults static checks could have caught and that the function meant to apply all 29 preflight checks was not called on the normal driver path. Code is MIT and the memory files, records and derived data are CC BY 4.0. The 676 raw frames (1.84 GB) and raw session transcripts are not in the repository, and the separate deposit has no DOI or link yet. The acquisition scripts are specific to the Asylum Research/Igor instrument they ran on and are published as a record of what ran; the physical results come from a small number of areas on one film, with retention followed for about an hour.

records.name: ABLE
records.domain: Dual-use protein-design tool use by LLM agents
records.inputs: Self-contained natural-language task prompts with defined tool sets (web search, Biopython, a ProteinMPNN-loaded cloud instance, AlphaFold3 output files) and, where relevant, the correct answers from previous steps
records.outputs: Per-task scores on a 0-1 scale (algorithmic grading, model-graded rubric for ABLE0), refusal and early-stopping rates, and comparison against a timed human expert baseline
records.notes: SecureBio benchmark that splits a computational protein-design workflow into nine tasks: one plan-generation task (ABLE0) and eight sequential execution tasks (ABLE1-8) spanning Protein Data Bank structure retrieval and preparation, ProteinMPNN sequence generation and validation of AlphaFold3 outputs, implemented on the UK AI Security Institute's Inspect AI framework. Fifteen frontier models were assessed ten times per task; seven named closed-weight models refused every task. Three tasks (ABLE0, ABLE6, ABLE8) were also run by 11 recruited domain experts with 1, 4 and 2 hours allocated and AI assistants prohibited. For dual-use reasons the authors do not share the full prompts or the ABLE0 rubric and redact the target pathogen, the properties modified and the scoring mechanism, so there is no runnable release and no benchmark artifact to licence (the preprint itself is CC BY 4.0). The single arXiv version (v1, 5 September 2026) carries an author comment that the manuscript was last revised in February 2026, an earlier revision having been presented at the NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Biosecurity Safeguards for Generative AI. The benchmark measures tool use on a redacted proxy workflow and the authors state it does not include wet-lab validation.

records.name: NS-Copilot
records.domain: Neuroscience data analysis with pre-trained neural models (EEG and extracellular spikes)
records.inputs: Raw neural recordings (NWB, EEGLAB, MATLAB or CSV) and a natural-language analysis task
records.outputs: Selected pre-trained models, generated analysis code, metrics, per-attempt audit logs and interpretive reports
records.notes: Multi-agent system from Case Western Reserve University (Planner, Coder, Controller, Interpreter) that chooses among nine integrated EEG and spike models and runs generated code in a Docker sandbox. When no model beats a performance threshold (by default the score of an independent GPT-5.2-Codex run), it replans or patches code for up to two retry rounds. Evaluated on one public dataset each for Alzheimer's EEG, Parkinson's EEG and working-memory spike decoding; the paper reports that forced retries were near-neutral on AD and lowered PD scores, and the system returns the best round. The arXiv record states acceptance to Findings of EMNLP 2026. Code is MIT; integrated model weights keep their own terms (the README lists NDT3 weights as CC-BY-NC-4.0 and REVE weights under a custom licence). Runs need an OpenAI API key, and auto mode also calls the Codex CLI. Closure is computational analysis of supplied data, with no hypothesis generation or wet-lab loop.

records.name: EvoSCM
records.domain: Causal-model hypothesis revision through in-silico experimentation (physics, materials, gene-regulatory networks)
records.inputs: A simulated scientific environment with an experiment interface, observations and configured LLM backends
records.outputs: Evolved structural causal model hypotheses, an executable law with a natural-language explanation, per-round experiment records and evaluation scores
records.notes: Method from Sun Yat-sen University and Tsinghua Shenzhen International Graduate School that keeps a population of structural causal model hypotheses, designs discriminative experiments and revises the models when predictions fail. The paper evaluates it on DiscoverPhysics, LLEMA and ActiveSciBench-GRN. The MIT-licensed release builds on the DiscoverPhysics simulator and agent code and covers only the 11 public DiscoverPhysics worlds (N-body backend), not the materials or gene-network adapters. All closure is in silico: simulators, and for materials a pretrained ALIGNN property oracle. Runs need hosted LLM APIs, and explanation scores come from a separate LLM judge. Builds on the DiscoverPhysics benchmark already in the catalog.

records.name: AgenticAI cross-tissue protein co-abundance pipeline
aliases: Agentic AI uncovers conserved cross-tissue protein co-abundance programs inaccessible to single-dataset analysis
records.domain: Cross-tissue proteomic co-abundance network comparison and hypothesis generation
records.inputs: ProteomicsDB tissue iBAQ protein-abundance data, plus UniProt, HPA, hu.MAP 3.0, g:Profiler, STRING, MyGene.info, Open Targets, Europe PMC and web-search lookups
records.outputs: Tissue co-abundance networks, conserved cross-tissue modules, database annotations and per-tissue-pair markdown research reports
records.notes: Notebook pipeline by Guan et al. (UIUC School of Information Sciences and University of Michigan; contact Haohan Wang). Four Hugging Face smolagents code agents build tissue co-abundance networks, extract modules conserved across tissue pairs, annotate them from public databases and write research reports. It was applied to all 820 pairs of 41 human tissues and fluids and found 1,833 conserved clusters in 406 pairs. Each agent follows a prescribed step list, and the operator runs the stages cell by cell, choosing tissues or pairs by editing loop filters. The significance tests, figures and published case-study narratives come from the authors' own code and writing. The paper does not evaluate the agents' accuracy. The authors present the agent as an evidence-integration layer, and its mechanistic hypotheses have no wet-lab validation. Running it requires a Hugging Face Inference token (configured for Qwen3.5-397B-A17B) and preprocessed data from the authors' Google Drive. Code GPL-3.0.

records.name: Agentic AFM (EPFL LBNI)
aliases: Agentic AI for operating scientific instruments for nanoscale characterization
records.domain: Atomic force microscope operation, image-based tuning and post-processing
records.inputs: Operator-defined imaging intent in natural language, live AFM height, error and KPFM channels, and instrument-control tools exposed over MCP
records.outputs: Ambiguity-checked instrument commands, bounded imaging-parameter updates, tuned AFM images, post-processed images and session reports
records.notes: EPFL Laboratory for Bio- and Nano-Instrumentation (Fantner group) framework of three MCP agents: AFM Messenger turns operator instructions into ambiguity-checked commands, AFM Pilot tunes setpoint, integral gain and scan rate from live height and error images, and AFM Doctor post-processes images with pre-approved tools. On a custom open-hardware AFM, AFM Pilot ran iterative acquire-assess-adjust loops on a calibration grating, a butterfly wing and a KPFM sample. In a paired comparison with five human operators from identical detuned starts (setpoint and integral gain only, scored with the agent's AI-vision rubric), both reached the predefined artifact thresholds; with n = 5 the Wilcoxon test cannot reach p < 0.05, so this shows similar outcomes in a small sample. Disclosed gates: humans set the experimental intent and resolve ambiguous commands, approach and scan start need operator confirmation, and tuning stays within operator-set bounds; the authors call it instrument operation, not a self-driving lab. Agent code and benchmark data are promised on publication; the cited repositories were not public on 2026-10-10.

records.name: SWE-bench Science
records.domain: Repository-level scientific software engineering by coding agents
records.inputs: Real scientific-software repositories at fixed baseline commits with issue-driven, expert-exploratory or engineering-integration task instructions and public tests
records.outputs: Agent patches applied in a separate clean verifier container (rebuilt for compiled projects) and scored by held-out private tests: public and private scores, Fail2Pass, Pass2Pass and binary pass@1
records.notes: Shanghai Innovation Institute and Fudan University (OpenMOSS) benchmark of 119 tasks from 98 GitHub repositories across 20 scientific domains; the best reported agent, Claude Code with Opus-5 (max), reaches 47.90% pass@1. Project tooling is MIT; task sources, instructions and image contents keep their upstream licences. Per-task environment and verifier images (with held-out tests and graders) are public on Docker Hub, and runs use the third-party Pier runner. 23 tasks with GPL-family, non-commercial or restricted-material upstream terms are excluded unless explicitly opted in. It measures repository-level repair and integration of scientific code, not end-to-end research, and is distinct from SciCode.

access_evidence.software_license: MIT (root LICENSE, OpenMOSS (SII)) for project-owned tooling and documentation; HF dataset card tagged MIT. Per NOTICE.md, upstream-derived task metadata, instructions, source snapshots and image contents keep upstream licences; held-out tests and graders ship in public Docker Hub verifier images without a separately stated licence. 23 opt-in tasks are GPL-family (18), non-commercial (2) or restricted-material (3).

records.name: GoalEvolve
records.domain: Electronic design automation: goal-driven evolution of OpenROAD physical-design algorithms
records.inputs: OpenROAD source snapshot, design and technology inputs, a frozen multi-objective QoR target region and a bounded editable source scope
records.outputs: Evolved OpenROAD C++ source variants with full-flow post-route QoR records, validity checks and mechanism evidence
records.notes: Fudan University system for evolving chip physical-design algorithms. Given a frozen multi-objective QoR target, the framework converts unmet targets into normalized gaps and uses stage-resolved checkpoint evidence to locate the bottleneck stage; an LLM Teacher then narrows the search to an algorithmic decision and source region, and parallel Codex-based Student agents edit, build and evaluate bounded OpenROAD C++ changes through a checkpointed post-placement optimization and global-routing flow. Reported on eight ASAP7 designs against default OpenROAD and commercial-tool targets; closure is computational only, and humans fix the goal contract, editable source scope and evaluation flow. The BSD-3-Clause repository includes replay artifacts for the eight evolved sources, while new campaigns need the Codex CLI and a model-provider API key. The domain is engineering algorithm discovery for chip physical design.

records.name: The Little Scientist
records.domain: Hypothesis-driven algorithm discovery on computational-biology benchmarks (protein fitness prediction, DNA motif discovery)
records.inputs: A benchmark with an automated evaluator returning per-instance diagnostics, a problem description and function signature, and optional human-supplied input data
records.outputs: Iterated scoring algorithms with logged hypotheses, predictions and evaluation history; final algorithms such as the Delta V ensemble strategy and the DALE motif finder
records.notes: Single-author framework (Travis Smith), called SEF (Scientific Experiment Framework) in the delta-v repository. A Scientist agent cycles through hypothesis, prediction, implementation, benchmark evaluation and reconciliation; a Kuhn agent injects a paradigm-shifting conjecture paired with a cross-disciplinary inspiration when progress plateaus. Agents run via cron on the OpenClaw platform with GLM-4.7. Reported outputs are Delta V, which the paper ranks first on the ProteinGym DMS substitutions zero-shot leaderboard (self-reported; the leaderboard pull request was still open and unmerged on 2026-10-10), and DALE, a DNA motif finder with higher mean AUROC than STREME across 132 ENCODE ChIP-seq datasets (0.842 vs 0.803); the agent wrote DALE in Python and the best version was ported to C for the benchmark. Closure is computational only. The human designed the evaluation infrastructure, rebuilt it after the first motif search stalled, supplied the five-model predictions behind the largest ProteinGym gain, and can trigger Kuhn cycles; the repository setup guide says the Scientist-to-Kuhn handoff is run manually or by a main OpenClaw agent. Both repositories are Apache-2.0. Orchestration scripts and Scientist/Kuhn prompts are released only for the ProteinGym case, in little-scientist-delta-v. The paper's code statement points the framework to little-scientist-dale, which holds only the motif agent prompt and best strategy, and the archived search history the paper places in delta-v is not in that repository.

records.name: AutoResearchEval
records.domain: Process-level failure diagnosis of end-to-end autonomous research agents across seven scientific domains
records.inputs: Research queries derived from published papers (premise and open tension, with the paper's key claims and conclusion withheld), plus agent trajectories and produced artifacts for judging
records.outputs: Failure labels under the 45-pattern AutoResearch Failure Taxonomy (ARFT), per-stage judge analyses, and optimization scores against source-paper results
records.notes: Built by Prentis AI (author affiliations also include Stanford University and Titan Holdings): 100 tasks from published papers in chemistry, geophysics, materials science, physics, scientific computing, biology and medicine. 70 are open-ended discovery tasks from 2024-onward papers; 30 are target-anchored optimization tasks that follow NatureBench's task selection. The CC BY 4.0 Hugging Face dataset holds the task files and 800 agent trajectories with per-rollout outcome metadata from eight harness-model pairs (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI). Per-trajectory ARFT labels are not in the dataset, although the paper states that annotations are released. The artifact-aware judge is MIT-licensed and on PyPI as autoresearcheval; its first stage needs an authenticated Claude Code CLI. The rest of the GitHub code has no licence file. The container rollout environment, including the held-out data and evaluation service for the optimization tasks, is not released. Judge agreement is reported only in aggregate over 50 calibration trajectories. This is a different resource from AutoResearchBench and EvoMap AutoResearch.

records.name: VALG
records.domain: Machine-learning theory: theorem formulation and graph-structured proof development
records.inputs: An ML-theory research direction or open problem, with an optional research brief
records.outputs: Literature surveys, perspective branches, theorem contracts, reviewed proof graphs and LaTeX theorem-candidate reports
records.notes: University of Hong Kong system released as an MIT-licensed bundle of 17 Codex skills (a controller, stage skills and shared templates) that runs inside Codex with subagents, without a standalone runtime; the archived runs used gpt-5.6-sol. Separate reviewer subagents diagnose failed proofs, and the controller routes each failure to derivation, proof-structure or theorem-formulation repair; formulation failures produce explicitly related variants or relaxations. On nine subproblems from five COLT 2026 open problems, two runs reached internally finalized candidates matching the source scope; checking was by LLM reviewers plus a rough human audit, without formal verification. Disclosed gate: the default interactive mode places a human-expert checkpoint after each pre-proof stage, and the archived run logs record such checkpoint decisions; autopilot approves by default and was used for the later stages of one run.

records.name: Periodic Neon (Periodic Labs)
records.domain: Agentic powder X-ray diffraction phase analysis in materials-synthesis labs searching for superconductors and magnets
records.inputs: Powder XRD patterns with synthesis context such as precursors, conditions and related experiments
records.outputs: XRD phase analyses of multiphase samples (which phases formed and in what proportions) with reasoning over competing phase hypotheses
records.notes: Periodic Labs midtrained the open-weight, trillion-parameter Kimi K2.6 on a blend of academic literature, code and experimental data, then applied reinforcement learning on its own lab data. The resulting model, Periodic Neon, runs in the Periodic Harness, which provides laboratory context, in-house structure and simulation databases and XRD analysis software. The company reports that Neon is deployed in its high-throughput labs to analyse XRD results. Its reported 55.3% success on the internal 134-sample FrontierXRD set is scored by an LLM-judge ensemble calibrated against expert ratings. Evidence is company posts only, with no paper, and no public release of the model, harness or benchmark was found. The September 2026 posts present AI direction of campaigns, synthesis and experiment choice as work being extended, and they demonstrate no AI-directed physical loop.

records.name: FARS
records.domain: AI/ML research (AI-for-AI)
records.inputs: Seed AI/ML research directions (nine in the public deployment); no interactive user input during execution
records.outputs: Hypotheses, plans, code, experiment logs, results and complete short papers, with per-project artifacts committed to GitLab
records.notes: Built by Analemma. Stage-specific agents for ideation, planning, experimentation and writing share a workspace and run each project without human intervention during execution. The first public deployment ran 417 hours on a 160-GPU cluster from nine seeded directions and produced 166 papers across 67 AI/ML topics. Before arXiv submission, a small selected subset got a minimal human integrity review that left the research content unchanged. Volunteer reviews (282 reviews of 140 papers) found review-worthy outputs alongside recurring narrow scope, methodological limits and integrity issues. The system code is not released, and the analemma.ai platform was unreachable in checks on 2026-08-13 and 2026-10-10. All 166 deployment papers, with human and LLM reviews, are on Hugging Face under Apache-2.0. Per-project artifacts are public on GitLab, without a licence.

records.name: SFitterAgents
records.domain: LHC analysis re-casting and global SMEFT fits (particle physics)
records.inputs: A published LHC measurement (arXiv paper or HEPData record) and the SMEFT operators of interest
records.outputs: Reviewed measurement extractions, MadGraph SM and SMEFT predictions, validated SFitter datacards, global-fit intervals and provenance records
records.notes: Built at Universität Heidelberg (Diefenbacher, Plehn, Schiller, Schmal) on top of MadGraphTeam's MadAgents (v3); the repository bundles the SFitter fitting code with a Claude Code multi-agent system. In the paper the agents proposed, re-simulated and fitted an ATLAS differential ttZ measurement into the top-sector global SMEFT analysis, with every step supervised by a physicist; closure is computational only. MIT licence; third-party components keep their own terms. Running it needs the Claude Code CLI with a Claude subscription or API credits, Apptainer, and a SLURM cluster with GPU nodes for real re-interpretations.

records.name: LAMMPS-Agents
aliases: Multi-Agentic AI Framework for End-to-End Atomistic Simulations
records.domain: Natural-language-driven LAMMPS atomistic simulation of materials properties
records.inputs: Natural-language materials-property request; OpenAI API key; local (or configured HPC) LAMMPS installation
records.outputs: Atomic structures, reviewed LAMMPS inputs, executed simulations and analysed properties (lattice and elastic constants, phonon dispersion, melting point) with vision-model checks of OVITO renderings
records.notes: AutoGen multi-agent framework from Argonne National Laboratory (Center for Nanoscale Materials and ALCF) with UIC. Specialised agents build structures, find interatomic potentials (with a web-surfer agent), write and review LAMMPS inputs, run simulations and analyse results; the analysis agent uses a vision model to check OVITO renderings and plots. The shipped code runs LAMMPS locally; an HPC module for Argonne's cluster is included but mostly disabled. Published in Digital Discovery (2026). The MIT-licensed GitHub repository, maintained by first author Katerina Vriza, is linked from the authors' Zenodo code record; agent chat logs and human-expert comparison runs are on Zenodo. Closure is computational only: the public code asks a human for input at every turn of the LAMMPS input-creator agent and ships a memory built from human teachings. Autonomy is rated from code and abstract because the article page was not machine-readable.

records.name: Finch
records.domain: Notebook-based analysis of biological experimental and omics data
records.inputs: Dataset(s) plus a natural-language research question or requested analysis
records.outputs: Executed Jupyter notebook (Python, R or Bash) with analyses, figures and a final answer
records.notes: FutureHouse data-analysis agent built on Aviary that iteratively writes and runs Jupyter-notebook code. It generated the BixBench agent trajectories and is the data-analysis component of Robin, which can launch ten independent Finch trajectories on wet-lab data. The public repository (formerly data-analysis-crow) is Apache-2.0, with releases v1.0.0 and v1.5.0 (September 2025). Edison Scientific hosts it as the Analysis agent (client alias JobNames.FINCH); the hosted version is documented with extra protein and figure tools and may differ from the public code. Closure is computational; experiments and data upload stay with the scientist.

decisions.name: GeneBench-Pro
decisions.rationale: Important older system absent from the baseline and from held leads: OpenAI agentic benchmark (30 Jun 2026) for multistage computational-biology analysis. Official openai organisation package on Hugging Face is MIT and contains 10 public problems with data, ground truth and a reference grader; 119 problems are held out (50 with Artificial Analysis). A second copy under the ajh-oai account is tagged CC BY 4.0; the record should cite only the official openai package. openai.com announcement returned HTTP 403 to this agent, so the PDF and the official dataset were used as primary evidence.

identity.note: OpenAI technical report PDF (Li & Ho, dated June 30, 2026) resolves (HTTP 200, 22 pages) and describes GeneBench-Pro as the expanded successor of GeneBench. Not an arXiv preprint, so no withdrawal state to check. The report's Data availability section (PDF p.16) hyperlinks the Hugging Face dataset openai/genebench-pro-public-package, so the repo is author-endorsed; HF API shows author=openai, created 2026-06-26, last modified 2026-06-30, not gated. No baseline record or deprecated ID matches genebench (asa_identity.tsv, asa_deprecated_ids.json); predecessor GeneBench is also absent from the baseline. Same-name items found and NOT to be cited: an unrelated 2021 GitHub repo raduangelescu/GeneBench (DE-gene benchmarking framework), third-party HF copies (ajh-oai/genebench-pro-public-package tagged cc-by-4.0; ssswwwxxx/genebench-pro) and a third-party Harbor adapter (josancamon19/sci-benches). The openai.com announcement page returned 403 in this check as well.

scope.note: In scope as an agent benchmark: each of 129 problems requires an agent in an offline Docker sandbox (Python/R, genomics tooling) to explore staged data, make 3-13 dependent analysis decisions (median 6) and return a JSON estimate graded pass/fail. This is multi-step computational analysis, comparable to BixBench/BixBench3/scBench-Long already in the catalog.

autonomy.note: B is correct: it is a benchmark. No physical or laboratory loop; all data are simulated.

access.note: LICENSE file in the official package is MIT ('Copyright (c) 2026 OpenAI'); README front matter and HF tags say license: mit. Only 10 of 129 problems are public (prompts, staged data, eval_config with ground truth and tolerances, reference_grader.py, report PDFs); 50 went to Artificial Analysis and 69 are internal; the package contains no agent runner or container. 'open-data' matches catalog precedent for partial benchmark releases with a permissive licence but no released harness (scBench-Long, QCV). The CC BY 4.0 tag on the ajh-oai copy conflicts with the official MIT licence; the record should cite only the openai-org package.

text.note: One factual error in notes: 'Staged data are synthetic or of stated uncertain provenance'. The report says all problems are constructively simulated from known data-generating processes (PDF p.7). The README claims prompts use 'Data provenance is uncertain', but all 10 public eval_config task texts actually say 'These data came from a real experiment', and none contain the uncertain-provenance statement (checked all 10). Also worth stating: ground truth is intentionally public, and no runner/harness is in the package. Counts (129 problems, 10 primary domains, 10 public, 50 Artificial Analysis, remainder internal = 69) and the GeneBench-successor claim are correct. Inputs/outputs are accurate; added 'offline' and the pass/fail tolerance grading.

identity.note: arXiv 2501.10385 resolves (abs 200; API 200): 'Autonomous Microscopy Experiments through Large Language Model Agents', Mandal ... Gosvami, Krishnan; v1 18 Dec 2024, v2 7 Jul 2025, no withdrawal text. arXiv HTML returns 404. The published version has a different title, 'Evaluating large language model agents for automation of atomic force microscopy' (Crossref 200: Nature Communications 16:9104, issued 2025-10-14, CC BY 4.0; same 8 authors; DOI resolves 200 to nature.com). PMC12521570 (200) is the same article and its Code availability statement names github.com/M3RG-IITD/AILA, so the repo is author-endorsed (org M3RG-IITD, not a fork; release AILA-0.1 published 2025-08-11 by first author imandal98; README carries the Nature Communications citation and a Zenodo DOI badge). No AFMBench/AILA/M3RG/2501.10385 entry in asa_identity.tsv or asa_deprecated_ids.json. Held lead 2608.26198 is a different EPFL LBNI system (different authors, different repo slug) and not a duplicate. Correction: the proposed name 'AFMBench (AILA)' with aliases 'AILA' and 'Artificially Intelligent Lab Assistant' merges the benchmark with the agent framework. Catalog precedent (AutoMat as an A3 row, STEM2Mat-Bench split out as a B row 'so system capability and evaluation evidence are not flattened into one row') and the proposer's own note that AILA may get a separate appraisal both argue for naming this row 'AFMBench' and keeping AILA out of its aliases, otherwise a later AILA agent row would collide on the alias.

scope.note: In scope as an agent benchmark: 100 hand-written AFM tasks graded on an LLM multi-agent framework that retrieves vendor documentation, writes and executes Python against the instrument API, and analyses images; 69% of tasks need multiple tools, 17% need multi-agent coordination (PMC, AFMBench section). Same lane as LabBench (robotic chemistry) and STEM2Mat-Bench.

autonomy.note: B is correct for a benchmark row. Physical execution is real for instrument-operation tasks (DriveAFM via Python API; AFM Handler engaged in 66 tasks), but not for every task: question_50 (fetched) asks the agent to open the stored file Glass_NAP.nid and plot it, i.e. offline analysis, so the proposed note 'AFMBench tasks are executed on a physical Nanosurf DriveAFM' overgeneralises the authors' own framing. Disclosure gaps under MAINTENANCE.md: documentation for critical operations was withheld from the agents and 'limited to trained human experts'; a human review step for risky actions 'was not implemented in AILA'; agents performed unrequested 'potentially risky tip movements'. Corrected notes add these. The AILA agent's own physical closure (PID optimisation on a calibration grid, friction series, graphene and indenter experiments) is real-instrument work and would argue for roughly A3-A5 in a separate physics-lane row; not appraised here.

access.note: open-source confirmed. GitHub API repos/M3RG-IITD/AILA: license spdx_id MIT; /license endpoint returns LICENSE.md with full MIT text, 'Copyright (c) 2025 Multiphysics and Multiscale Mechanics Research Group (M3RG), IIT Delhi'; raw LICENSE.md 200. Zenodo archive of release AILA-0.1 (record 16793993) also states MIT. Repo tree holds Data/afm_qs/question_1..100.json, Data/task.py, app/ (AILA_3.5/4.0/claude/llama scripts) and Results/ (Single-Agent, Multi-Agent per model, Real_1, Real_2, MCP, Load experiment). Practical gate, not a licence gate: instrument tasks need a Nanosurf DriveAFM and its vendor Python API (code calls nanosurf.SPM()), plus paid LLM API keys; the README asks users to paste their own key. access_evidence stays null as for other MIT rows.

category.note: benchmark is correct for this row (precedent: STEM2Mat-Bench, LabBench robotic chemistry). A separate AILA agent row would fall under physics, matching TEM Agent, AEcroscopyWave and CALMS.

access.note: 'open-source' is NOT supported. The MIT licence is real (LICENSE file and GitHub API spdx MIT) but the licensed repository contains only README, CITATION.cff, three docs files, four GIFs and empty training/ and testing/ folders. README: 'This repository is documentation. The generator, oracle, scorer and harness ... live in the source tree (Coming Soon)'. The benchmark runs through a prebuilt Harbor image whose licence is not stated. This contradicts the paper's statement that 'DrugTargetWorld code is publicly available' at the repo. The released artifact is the world data on Hugging Face: LICENSE.md states generated tables and oracle state are MIT and ACDC-derived cine-MRI is under ACDC terms (registration, no redistribution); the whole dataset is gated (HF gated=auto, card licence 'other'/'drugtargetworld-mixed') and the benchmark build stops without an HF token after accepting the gate. Catalog precedent for released task data with an unreleased harness is 'open-data' (asa-scbench-long; cf. asa-bixbench3 for upstream data terms), so access should be 'open-data' with the gate and unreleased source disclosed in notes. If the maintainer reads the third-party ACDC gate as incompatible with 'open-data', the fallback is HOLD until the source tree is released, not 'open-source'.

scope.note: Agent builds, executes, repairs and replays typed tool/code workflows on scientific tasks with evaluators and hard constraints, then updates its own Skill/Operator program; plus a companion benchmark of continual self-evolution. Multi-step computational scientific work, in scope. Caveat: several of the 23 task families are ML-style tasks (code generation, music source separation, OCR post-correction) mapped to ANZSRC divisions, so 'scientific work' is broad here.

autonomy.note: A3 supported. Tasks are supplied with objective, inputs, evaluator and constraints; the agent constructs and repairs the workflow and the batch evolver promotes updates through an automatic replay-and-validation gate (70 of 161 candidates in the paper's seven rounds). No hypothesis generation or open-ended research loop, so not A4; purely computational, so not A5. Human gate must be disclosed: in gateway (live) use, candidates wait as 'ready' until the user promotes them, and every promotion can be rolled back (README).

Only v1 exists and the abs page has no withdrawal notice. The paper's Data and code availability section names github.com/BIABench/BIABench (BSD 3-Clause) and HF BIABench/BIABench (DOI 10.57967/hf/10561, which redirects to the HF dataset). The repo README and biabench.github.io link back to the arXiv ID, so the artifacts are author-endorsed in both directions. No BIABench or bioimage record exists in baseline asa_identity.tsv, asa_deprecated_ids.json or agents_final.json. Possible name confusion: baseline 'BioInformatics Agent (BIA)' (asa-bioinformatics-agent-bia, bioRxiv 2024.05.22.595240) is a different system. BIABench's 'BIA' stands for bioimage analysis, so this is not a rename or duplicate.

scope.note: This is an agent benchmark and harness: 16 end-to-end bioimage-analysis tasks rebuilt from published studies, and agents must choose and run multi-step pipelines (segmentation, tracking, colocalization, stitching and others) on raw 2D, 3D and time-lapse data. It falls within the catalog's 'benchmarks/harnesses that evaluate such systems' boundary.

autonomy.note: B is correct: it is a benchmark/harness. The paper reports three runs per agent-task pair, no system prompt beyond the task instruction and unrestricted network access, with outputs scored against ground truth and by a VLM judge.

access.note: The open-source licence is confirmed in three places. scope.note: In scope as a benchmark/harness for agents doing multi-step ML development, on the same precedent as asa-mle-bench and asa-mle-dojo. It is more than a one-off audit: it releases a reusable toolkit that converts any command-line agent run into a labelled trajectory and reports it against human cohorts, plus 'traceml record', which runs an agent under a recorder with MLE-bench grading. Caveat for the curator: it measures development process, not outcomes, and covers Kaggle-style ML engineering only (no wet-lab or natural-science tasks).

scope.note: Borderline but within precedent. The harness runs a multi-round hypothesis -> probe -> feedback -> revision loop and scores rule reports and held-out answers, framed by the authors as evaluating scientific exploration and positioned against DiscoveryWorld, NewtonBench and SciLaws-Bench. Precedent: DiscoveryWorld (fictional worlds), Science Sandboxes/CodonBox (invented biological rules), ChemWorld, plus non-natural-science research benchmarks (MLE-bench, RE-Bench). Caveats that reduce fit: both worlds are an alien programming language and a patched natural-deduction logic with no science-domain content; the README places it third in the authors' series on test-time learning (EvaLearn, CL-bench); the Limitations section says it measures rule acquisition in synthetic environments, 'not whether they can conduct real scientific discovery'. If the curator reads scope strictly as science-domain benchmarks, this is the entry to drop.

README License section also states Apache-2.0. Release boundary: harness, scoring, evaluation engines, analysis scripts and two small demo worlds are public; the two evaluation worlds (rules and test instances) are private and the README states they are not shared with individual researchers, so leaderboard-comparable scores need a maintainer-run evaluation. This mirrors the ASI-Bench precedent (open code, official scoring through maintainers) but is stricter, since the scored task set itself is unavailable; the notes must say so.

scope.note: In scope as a benchmark/harness. The Active track is a multi-step tool loop: the model gets only a subfield name, issues up to 10 Semantic Scholar SEARCH/FETCH calls, then emits FINAL with a hypothesis; every tool call is logged. The Static track is single-pass, but the benchmark's purpose is the matched Static-vs-Active comparison of agentic literature exploration plus hypothesis generation. Catalog precedent: IdeaBench, HypoBench and ResearchBench are listed as B ideation/hypothesis benchmarks. Weakness to note: it evaluates one stage of the scientific workflow (ideation), and the hypotheses are never tested.

autonomy.note: B is correct (benchmark). No physical or experimental closure is claimed; the README and data card state that the hypotheses are untested model output scored by other models.

text.note: (1) The outputs field says '558 structured trajectories recording thoughts, tool calls…'. That overstates the public release. The HF dataset (lastModified 2026-04-16, five days before the GitHub commit 'Final submission: 558 trajectories, n=363 LLM-judged evaluation, tool-scaffolded open-weight') holds 372 frontier + 120 open-weight + 30 live-retrieval = 522 trajectory files in its structured folders, plus 251 older pilot files under data/trajectories. The paper's 60 live-retrieval variants (released stats say n_trajectories 30, live_pubmed_hits 2) and its 6 tool-scaffolded Qwen trajectories were not found on HF or GitHub. The 120 open-weight trajectories are single responses with no tool calls (sample: total_steps 1, total_tool_calls 0). The median frontier trajectory is 2 steps (paper Table 2), and 4 of 8 frontier files I sampled were single-step. The HF card itself still says 432 trajectories. (2) The 'Best Dataset Award' claim comes from the authors (README, arXiv comment, paper footnote, certificate image). The workshop schedule independently confirms only an oral slot ('Dataset & AI Scientist Highlights Block 1', #142); the fetched workshop pages do not name award winners. The award belongs to the workshop's Dataset Proposal Competition, which solicits 2-page proposals, and the notes should say so. (3) 'Several reported success rates rely on LLM judging' understates the problem. All headline success rates (84-89%, n=363) are cross-model LLM-judged. Those labels are not in the public release: medium/hard trajectory files carry verification method 'pending'. The released results/statistics/reviewer_analysis_results.json still reports ground-truth-only claim verification on n=42-43 per model (~69%), and the HF card says ~69%, p=0.997. The error taxonomy uses keyword heuristics (paper Appendix E). (4) The notes omit that the harness's web_search is a placeholder ('Simulate web search using the model's knowledge') and that api_call targets other than PubChem and UniProt return a 'simulated' note; the paper confirms simulated web search for the frontier trajectories. (5) Inputs: the open-weight models ran only 30 drug-discovery easy/medium tasks, not all 124. The '124 tasks' figure applies to the frontier models.

scope.note: Benchmark of AI research agents that inspect workflow code, adaptively buy a limited number of experimental measurements and deliver a predicted response surface; this is multi-step experiment design and inference. Workflows are ML/computational tasks (classification, regression, clustering, forecasting, image restoration, retrieval, beat detection, link prediction). In scope on catalog precedent for ML-research agent benchmarks (MLAgentBench, MLE-bench, RE-Bench, EXP-Bench, FML-bench) and Auto-Bench (iterative intervention discovery). Caveat: 'measurements' are served from exhaustively precomputed native outcomes, so agents query an evaluator rather than launching new runs.

autonomy.note: B is correct for a benchmark/harness. The paper evaluates DeepSeek V4 Flash/Pro agents plus numerical baselines (ridge, GP); no system-level autonomy claim to assess.

No deprecated id matches. Generic-acronym disambiguation in the display name is appropriate (T-REX/T-REx is used by unrelated NLP and tooling projects).

scope.note: In scope: a long-horizon agentic campaign controller that executes multi-step scientific work (simulation/tool execution, evaluation, evidence accumulation, reporting). Planner and Supervisor LLM agents reason over accumulating outcomes and propose/prioritise jobs; a deterministic controller validates and schedules generation, redesign and evaluation jobs across six generation tools (four Proteina-Complexa variants, BindCraft, BoltzGen) plus ProteinMPNN redesign and AF2 evaluation. Campaign archives record evidence summaries, hypothesis cards, action candidates, supervisor decisions, launch/dispatch records and provenance, and 'trex status'/'trex export' produce analysis and ranked output manifests. This is not a base-model family, an optimisation library, a single scientific software component, or a one-off case-study audit.

autonomy.note: A3-A4 is supported and correctly stops short of A5. Observed closure is in silico only: the paper states it evaluated T-REX in a computational setting with established in-silico metrics, and no wet-lab testing of T-REX designs is reported. Closure within a campaign is genuine and long-horizon (default README example is a 48-hour, multi-GPU Slurm campaign; the controller deterministically assigns campaign states, LLM agents propose and prioritise actions, and no human-in-the-loop or manual mid-campaign step is described in the methods text read). A4 upper bound rests on strategy-level hypothesis/evidence artefacts and adaptive reallocation rather than formulation of novel scientific questions, so the range (not a flat A4) is the honest label; it is also consistent with baseline precedent (AutoBinder Agent A3-A4, AutoProteinEngine A3). Human gating consists only of ordinary job submission (trex check / trex submit), which the record's inputs field already reflects.

Repo is not a fork and not archived, created 2026-09-22, last push 2026-09-30, default branch main, 319 blobs including a substantive trex/ package (controller.py, critic.py, campaign/, evidence/, execution/, archive_schema.py), config/, slurm/, benchmarks/, docs/, examples/ — i.e. a real release, not a stub. The bioRxiv API lists only v1 (2026-09-17, 'new results', CC BY-NC-ND), titled 'Microscope control with a natural language agent' (Marin ... Schueder, Ries), with Zach Marin as corresponding author at Max Perutz Labs, University of Vienna. No withdrawal notice: the only 'withdraw' strings on the page belong to the cookie banner. The Code availability section names github.com/Micro-Claw/microclaw. The repo README and CITATION.cff cite the same preprint with the same author list, so the repo is author-endorsed. Not in the baseline: the baseline contains MolClaw, MatClaw, Dr. Claw, ResearchClawBench, the OpenClaw ecosystem and OpenClaw/Claw AI Lab/LabClaw, but no MicroClaw and no deprecated-ID match. Same-name collision OUTSIDE the catalog: microclaw/microclaw (MIT, 747 stars, created 2026-02-07) is an unrelated Rust chat assistant 'inspired by nanoclaw', and gh search shows several more unrelated 'MicroClaw' repos (OpenClaw installers, ESP32 agents). The proposal mentions this only in its rationale, so the record itself needs a disambiguation line. 'Ries laboratory' does not appear in the paper (affiliations list Max Perutz Labs/Vienna BioCenter, University of Vienna, plus EPFL, University of California and FH Upper Austria co-authors), so that wording should be dropped.

scope.note: Multi-step scientific work on real instruments: the agent plans acquisition sequences, writes and applies image-analysis hooks, calls ilastik, makes acquisition decisions (stage moves, channel/laser/dichroic switching, time-lapse when kinesin density is adequate), troubleshoots optical paths, and compiles sessions into reusable Pycro-Manager scripts. This is in scope for instrument-control agents, matching the precedents TEM Agent, AEcroscopyWave and the NV-center agent.

autonomy.note: A3-A5 is defensible and matches the TEM Agent precedent (A3-A5, open-source). The A5 upper bound rests on observed physical closure: in the kinesin demo it scanned a live-cell coverslip, detected microtubule networks with an agent-written hook, switched laser and dichroic, refocused and acquired time-lapses on real hardware, and in the mitochondria demo it scored ilastik FOVs and centred them. Most use is collaborative, though. The paper calls the system 'pseudo-agentic', and several demos still needed humans. In Exchange-PAINT the user added the washes and imagers. In the mitochondria demo the final SMLM data were collected by the authors with the Micro-Manager MDA wizard and htSMLM plugin. Gates that must be disclosed and are missing from the proposed notes: blocking user confirmations before enabling illumination and before acquisitions above thresholds (these can be granted for the rest of a session), and explicit user approval of every agent-written hook before it runs. The note also needs the safety_config hard gate, which the proposal already has. There is no hypothesis generation or experimental-design loop, so an A4/A5 reading as an 'autonomous scientist' would be inflated. The range is kept with the gates written into the notes.

access.note: open-source is confirmed. The GitHub API reports license spdx_id BSD-3-Clause. The LICENSE file text reads 'BSD 3-Clause License', copyright 2026 Microclaw contributors. CITATION.cff says BSD-3-Clause, and the paper's Code availability statement agrees. Caveats for the notes: the README marks the release 'PREVIEW ONLY' and NOT suitable for production, Windows 10/11 is the only tested platform, and a user-supplied Anthropic API key is required (the README names claude-opus-4-8). There are no GitHub releases, only the tag 'nikon-shipment-1'; the CITATION.cff version is 0.1.0. The data are on Zenodo under CC BY 4.0, and the code is not under an NC licence.

identity.note: bioRxiv 10.64898/2026.09.30.750244 resolves (abstract and full text HTTP 200; bioRxiv API: v1 only, dated 2026-10-01, type 'new results', published DOI 'NA', no withdrawal). Title 'An AI-powered cloud biofoundry for autonomous biological research'; corresponding author Huimin Zhao, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. The paper itself names the portal ('The iCloudBiofoundry platform is available at: https://icloudbiofoundry.illinois.edu'), so the platform link is author-endorsed. Not a duplicate: the baseline 'AI-native autonomous biofoundry' (asa-ai-native-autonomous-biofoundry) is a different preprint (10.64898/2026.02.01.703093) from MGI Tech (corresponding author Meng Yang). No other baseline or deprecated record matches iCloudBiofoundry, iBioGenie, BiofoundryAI, iBioFAB or the Zhao laboratory. GitHub repository search for the three names and an arXiv search for 'cloud biofoundry' returned nothing, so no same-name collision was found (search result, not proof of absence). The earlier Zhao-lab autonomous enzyme-engineering platform (Nat. Commun. 16, 5648, 2025), whose phytase data seeded case study 1, is not in the baseline either; it is a predecessor, not this system.

scope.note: Multi-step scientific work end to end: natural-language objective, literature/database/tool-driven design (iBioGenie), protocol generation, compilation into robotic workflows with digital-twin simulation (BiofoundryAI), execution on two UIUC biofoundries, and measurements returned to the user. Three wet-lab case studies plus computational benchmarks.

autonomy.note: A4-A5 is supported, but the human gates are heavier than the proposal states and must be disclosed. Physical closure is real: designed libraries were built and screened on iBioFAB/iBioFoundry (Tecan Fluent, Echo, PIXL colony picker, robotic arm, plate reader, EchoMS/LC-MS), and a second PAND design round built on round-1 measurements was executed robotically. Gates documented in the supplement: researchers approve plans before transfer to BiofoundryAI (p4); administrators approve every instrument job so 'no instrument job reaches hardware without explicit human authorization' (p6); deployment does not start runs, an operator completes physical setup and starts execution (p45); the authors selected the second-round PAND target (p76) and manually structured the 32-candidate list (p66); the phytase round was seeded with data from an earlier campaign that the authors supplied. Each case study was initiated by a human instruction. The proposal's rationale ('second design iteration driven by returned measurements') overstates agent-initiated iteration. Simulation-only closure is not what drives A5 here; the A5 end rests on the executed wet-lab runs.

access.note: lab-gated is kept. No source code is public: Code availability says code will be released 'upon acceptance', and the portal's own GitHub page data file lists four repositories (iBioFoundry/iBioFoundry-AI, iBioFoundry/BioFoundryAgent, iBioFoundry/cloud-biofoundry, iBioFoundry/ibiofoundry-helm) that all returned 404 via both the GitHub API and github.com on 2026-10-10 (private or not yet created). The iBioFoundry GitHub org has only two unrelated public repos (KcatNet, GPL-3.0; an issue tracker). The preprint licence is bioRxiv 'cc_no' (no reuse), which is a text licence, not a software licence. The portal is live but gated: the supplement says sign-in goes through CILogon federated SSO, and the portal bundle shows a profile form ('request access to the platform') and an 'Access pending approval' screen awaiting administrator approval; robotic execution needs the UIUC facilities, admin job approval and an on-site operator, and Momentum is a commercial Thermo Fisher product. 'platform' is a defensible alternative, but lab-gated matches catalog precedent (SAMPLE, AI-native autonomous biofoundry) and the legend 'needs robotic lab, institutional infrastructure'. access_evidence stays null (catalog uses it only for source-available).

category.note: biology is correct: synthetic biology (enzyme discovery/engineering, yeast metabolic engineering) on biofoundries; consistent with the baseline AI-native autonomous biofoundry and SAMPLE records.

urls.note: https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.09.30.750244v1 -> 200, matches the system. https://icloudbiofoundry.illinois.edu -> 200 (redirects to trailing slash), page title 'iCloudBiofoundry', client-rendered Angular shell; label 'Platform' is correct and the URL is named in the paper. No repository URL should be added: the four GitHub repos the portal lists are 404.

text.note: Facts in the proposed notes check out (UIUC/Zhao, iBioGenie and BiofoundryAI roles, iBioFAB and iBioFoundry, three case studies, code promised on acceptance, Momentum commercial). Corrections: (1) notes understate human gates ('Researchers review designs and plans' only); add admin approval of every instrument job, operator setup/start, author choice of the second-round target and manual finalisation of candidates; (2) state that the phytase round reused prior campaign data; (3) record the gated portal (federated sign-in plus admin-approved access request) and the 404 status of the four listed repositories; (4) outputs should say workflows run after administrator approval. Aliases iBioGenie and BiofoundryAI are component names, not alternate names for the whole system; kept for search/dedup since no collision was found.

identity.note: arXiv:2609.19099 resolves (abs, HTML, API all 200); single version v1, Wed 16 Sep 2026 17:31:27 UTC; no withdrawal notice; title 'Evidence-Grounded Agentic Formulation Development in an Autonomous Laboratory', authors Craig, Hickman, Ma, Piche-Taillefer, Allen, Bannigan, affiliation Intrepid Labs, Toronto. Paper names the system Andromeda 2 and matches both proposals. No 'Andromeda' or 'Intrepid' name, alias or deprecated id in baseline asa_identity.tsv / asa_deprecated_ids.json; no formulation-design record in agents_final.json. The two lane proposals ('Andromeda 2' in biology-medicine, 'Andromeda 2 (Intrepid Labs)' in chemistry-materials) are the SAME system and must be merged into one record. Naming risk inside the company: press material (lead only, not evidence) describes a commercial 'ANDROMEDA' as a proprietary ML model 'not a large language model' licensed to Quotient Sciences (Dec 2025); this appears to be the non-agentic Andromeda 1 comparator in the paper (inference, not confirmed). The record must therefore name Andromeda 2 explicitly and keep the parenthetical disambiguator, following the 'A-Lab (Berkeley)' precedent. An earlier related paper by the same group (ref [16], ICML 2026 AI for Science workshop, clofazimine) is linked to OpenReview, but OpenReview returned a bot-challenge page; it is UNVERIFIED and not added.

scope.note: Multi-step scientific work with a physical experimental loop: proposal, critique, review, planning and constraint-checking over a shared formulation context; tool calls to probabilistic models; deterministic feasibility engine; robot-prepared batches; automated assays; six sequential batches adapted from returned measurements; ablation and DoE/optimiser comparators. Not an optimisation library: the non-agentic optimiser (Andromeda 1) is the comparator, not the proposed entry.

autonomy.note: A4-A5 accepted (precedent: Chemist-X A4-A5). Physical closure is observed: six 16-formulation wet-lab batches per arm prepared by liquid-handling robots, automated dissolution/DLS/HPLC, measurements returned to the agent's working context for the next batch. Reasons not to grant plain A5: a formulation scientist reviewed every batch before execution (a gate, though explicitly without editing compositions); all arms used the same (human) operators and instruments; the paper does not show the agent directly driving robots or that data return was automatic (passive 'were returned to the system'). The human gate must be disclosed in notes (both proposals do).

access.note: lab-gated is correct. No code, model, data or availability statement found in the full text (my search of the HTML; describes the search, not proof of absence). Methods 4.3: models are developed, trained and operated on Intrepid infrastructure. CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 shown on arXiv is the PAPER licence, not a software licence; it must not be cited as access evidence. access_evidence should be omitted (schema type is object; null as proposed would fail validation). Admission under the paper-only/unreleased exception is justified by demonstrated physical-lab closure with a matched wet-lab comparator, as the September rule allows; weaknesses: single company preprint, one API, one campaign per arm, not peer reviewed.

category.note: chemistry fits catalog precedent for self-driving chemistry/materials labs (Ada, A-Lab, Chemist-X); the task is excipient-mixture composition design with physicochemical (in-vitro FaSSIF dissolution) endpoints, no biological assay. Biology lane already flagged it to chemistry.

urls.note: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.19099 (200) and https://arxiv.org/html/2609.19099 (200) both resolve and support identity, robotic execution, human gate and results. No repo/platform link proposed and none should be added: no official Intrepid product page was fetched as evidence; news/press items are leads only. Paper link label should follow catalog convention 'arXiv:2609.19099'.

text.note: Corrections needed. (1) Biology-lane notes claim the authors state 'nothing publicly released'; the paper says only that models are developed, trained and operated on Intrepid infrastructure and use no external commercial model APIs. Rephrase as 'the paper describes no code, model or data release'. Its source entry labels the 'Both platforms are fully in-house.' excerpt as supporting 'no public release', which overreaches. (2) 'proposal, critique, review and planning agents': the paper says these steps 'operate over a shared formulation context'; it does not say they are separate agents. (3) 'robot-measured' results: robots prepare the batches; the assays are automated. (4) Missing context that limits the headline numbers: 'high-AUC hit' is a relative threshold (pooled upper quartile of all paclitaxel formulations); each arm is a single campaign (authors state this limits inference); endpoint is in-vitro FaSSIF dissolution, which the authors say is not bioavailability. (5) Chemistry-lane notes are otherwise accurate (50/17/2%, 96 formulations, gate, operators). Merge into one record.

scope.note: Multi-step scientific work: LLM ReAct agents drive end-to-end single-particle cryo-EM processing in CryoSPARC (preprocessing, picking, 2D/3D optimisation, reconstruction, heterogeneity analysis, failure recovery via forum retrieval, exploration of alternative processing strategies), benchmarked on several EMPIAR datasets against deposited maps and cryoWizard. Reusable released system, not a case study.

autonomy.note: A3-A4 supported. Observed in-silico closure: rigid workflow + guided optimisation/heterogeneity agents with agent-chosen parameters and stopping (A3); hypothesis-driven exploration formulates processing-strategy hypotheses, executes CryoSPARC job sequences, compares resolution/cFAR and adopts or archives each branch (A4 upper bound). Caveats: the 'hypotheses' concern processing strategy, not biology; on EMPIAR-10181 exploration improved resolution only 'slightly but not very much'; the 60S state came from the guided heterogeneity agent, and the biological interpretation, model refinement and DRGN-AI cross-check were done by the authors. Not A5: input data are existing EMPIAR movies, no microscope or acquisition control (paper lists automated data acquisition as future extension). No human safety gates described; default run script runs guided then exploration automatically.

access.note: open-source confirmed: GitHub API license endpoint returns Apache-2.0 (spdx Apache-2.0, LICENSE file 201 lines of the Apache 2.0 text; raw LICENSE 200); README states Apache 2.0; lab Gitee mirror also Apache-2.0. Runtime dependencies are proprietary/external: a licensed CryoSPARC (tested <=4.7.1) and a DeepSeek/OpenAI/Panshi LLM API key; disclosed in notes. access_evidence not needed.

scope.note: In scope. Multi-step scientific work closed end to end: a ProteinNPT-based model proposes chimeric GH1 variants, a robotic laboratory assembles genes, expresses protein cell-free and runs fluorescence enzyme assays, measurements retrain the model and drive the next round's acquisition (UCB with MC-dropout uncertainty). Not a general model family, not a library, not a one-off case study. Also ships in-silico DMS benchmarks (Pab1, GB1, Ube4b, avGFP), but the system itself is the agent-plus-laboratory platform, so 'biology' rather than 'benchmark' is correct.

autonomy.note: A5 supported by observed physical closure, not by claim alone. Named hardware: Dynamic Devices Lynx LM730i liquid handler, Analytik Jena Biometra TRobot II thermal cycler, Agilent BioTek Synergy H1 plate reader, custom automated refrigerator, Peak Robotics KX2-750 arm. 25 rounds over about one month (Figure 3 legend panel h), 132 characterised variants, three agents on a shared model. Wet results are real, not simulated: purified-protein kinetics (kcat/Km) on glucose, xylose, mannose. Two human touch points are disclosed in the paper and should be visible in the record rather than smoothed over: the laboratory was stocked with all fragments and reagents before the campaign started (Methods), and top variants were manually re-assayed afterwards for verification (Results). Neither is a mid-loop intervention, so A5 stands. Note for the evidence trail, not for the record: the proposal's locator for the 25-round excerpt says 'Figure 1 legend, panel h'; the sentence is in the Figure 3 legend, panel h.

text.note: One factual slip in notes. The proposal writes that the Apache-2.0 code covers 'the agent, in-silico deep-mutational-scanning benchmarks and the laboratory-environment software, which can be run without hardware'. The README says the opposite about the environment: the agent and the benchmarks can be run with no laboratory hardware, while environment/ is the software that drives the physical instruments (lab_controller.py, a lab_config, auto-fridge firmware and wiring). Corrected. Everything else checks out: ProteinNPT-based model, three agents sharing one learning model, 25 rounds, about one month, Family 1 glycoside hydrolases, specificity shifted toward non-native sugars, SAMPLE as the group's earlier system, inputs (six parent enzymes, eight recombined fragments, roughly 1.7 million chimeras, three substrate objectives) and outputs (built and characterised variants plus an updated sequence-function model). No inflated numbers: the paper's own figures are modest for glucose (2.9-fold over the best parent) and the proposal does not quote fold changes at all. Alias trimmed to the paper's spelling of the expansion, and the two disclosed human touch points added.

Closest baseline neighbours are distinct systems - asa-plmeae (PLMeAE, HICAI-ZJU, s41467-025-56751-8), asa-sample (SAMPLE, Nat Chem Eng s44286-023-00002-4), asa-ai-native-autonomous-biofoundry (2026 bioRxiv, no repo) and asa-autoproteinengine (AutoML, A3). scope.note: In scope: a closed design-build-test-learn loop that proposes variants (ESM-2 protein language model plus the EVmutation epistasis model, then a low-N supervised model trained on each round's assay data), executes construction and characterisation on a robotic biofoundry, and feeds measured fitness back into the next round, with a GPT-based natural-language interface for campaign setup. Not a general LLM, not an optimisation library, not a one-off case study: two complete four-round engineering campaigns are reported.

autonomy.note: A5 supported by observed physical closure, not simulation: the robotic pipeline covers mutagenesis PCR, DNA assembly, transformation, colony picking, plasmid purification, protein expression and enzyme assays on the iBioFAB (Thermo F5 arm, Thermo Momentum scheduler), and 446 AtHMT and 448 YmPhytase variants were built and screened across four rounds in four weeks. Required disclosure added: the authors self-assess the platform as between level 3 (conditional automation) and level 4 (high automation) and describe steps within each module as needing 'little, if any, human intervention', i.e. module-level automation with some human involvement around module boundaries. Consistent with the A5 precedent already used for PLMeAE, SAMPLE and the AI-native autonomous biofoundry.

scope.note: Multi-step computational work with code execution and analysis: data exploration, splitting, representation, architecture design, training, inference, prediction exploration, then programmatic metric computation and an experiment-design LLM that plans the next iteration; ends with a PDF report. Fits catalog precedent for ML-engineering agents (AIDE A3, AutoProteinEngine A3, AIDO.Harness A4, MARS A3-A4). It produces predictive models, not hypotheses or experiments; the proposed notes already say so.

autonomy.note: A3-A4 supported by observed in-silico closure in the published paper (Algorithm 1, Sections 2.5-2.6): each iteration runs seven steps with validation-retry loops; train/validation metrics are computed programmatically; the experiment-design LLM uses all iteration summaries to instruct the next iteration; the best iteration by validation score is output. Evaluation: 20 datasets, 3 replicates x 8 h, GPT-5.1-Codex-Max backbone, test sets hidden from the agent. Human role is set-up only (run duration, LLM backbone, validation metric, split/baseline budgets). No physical loop, so not A5. Lower bound A3 is the conservative reading because the step sequence is predefined; A4 upper bound matches MARS/AIDO.Harness precedent.

access.note: REFUTED as proposed. The latchbio/scbench repo is genuinely Apache-2.0 (GitHub licence endpoint apache-2.0; LICENSE contains the full Apache 2.0 text; pyproject license Apache-2.0). That repo, though, holds only a thin CLI (scbench/cli.py, __init__.py, types.py), 6 eval JSONs, results and trajectories. scbench/__init__.py imports the graders (latch_eval_tools.graders) and the harness (latch_eval_tools.harness.EvalRunner, run_minisweagent_task), and the CLI imports batch_download_datasets from latchbio/latch-eval-tools, pinned as latch-eval-tools==0.3.10. GitHub detects no licence for it, and PyPI 0.3.10 declares no licence. The harness sat inside the Apache repo only from 2026-02-01 to 2026-02-04 (scbench/harness/ at init commit dd4e6df905) before PR #1 migrated it out, so already at paper time it lived outside the Apache repo; graders were always external. The proposal's claim that 'Framework, graders, linter and agent harness are Apache-2.0' is therefore false for the graders and harness. The functional benchmark is public code without an open licence, so the label should be source-available with access_evidence. identity.note: arXiv 2607.19262 resolves (abs 200, HTML 200, API 1 result): v1 only, submitted 2026-07-21, no withdrawal notice; title, LatchBio/Aclid affiliations and 100-evaluation design match. Repo latchbio/biosecbench-surveillance is owned by the LatchBio organisation, not a fork, and IS cited by the paper's Data availability section (the proposal's rationale wrongly says the paper does not cite it), so it is author-endorsed. README still says 'Paper: link pending'. No 'biosec'/'latch' hit in asa_identity.tsv except asa-scbench-long (different benchmark) and none in asa_deprecated_ids.json. Name-family to disambiguate: same group published BioSecBench-Refusal (arXiv 2607.05462, refusal/risk benchmark, cited as ref [11]) and has a latchbio/biosecbench-function repo; neither is in the baseline. Not a collision, but notes should name the sibling.

scope.note: In scope as an agent benchmark: agents get raw or near-raw sequencing data (FASTQ, contigs, alignments) in a containerised sandbox with bioinformatics tools and internet, must choose references, thresholds and workflows over many ungraded intermediate steps, and return a JSON answer graded deterministically. Comparable to BixBench/scBench-Long.

autonomy.note: B is correct. Benchmark only; no physical or laboratory loop. Runs were 16 model-harness pairs x 3 trials x 100 evaluations on LatchBio infrastructure, six-hour limit.

access.note: 'open-data' is not supported. The public repository contains only README, METHODS.md, docs/specification.md, a manifest, seven eval.json files (task prompt + descriptive metadata + canary) and two aggregate-results CSVs. Every eval.json states that input sequencing data, grader, solution notes and ground truth are withheld; no trajectories are released; the full 100-evaluation set is 'available to qualified partners' only. So no benchmark data that can run or score an agent is public, not even for the seven examples. The proposal's claimed precedent does not hold: scBench-Long released data_node pointers, answer vocabularies and full agent trajectories for its 4 public evaluations, and GeneBench-Pro (October) released staged data, ground truth and a reference grader for its 10 public problems. Licence itself is fine but not decisive: LICENSE is Apache-2.0 text with the appendix dropped and the phrase '(except as stated in this section)' missing from section 3, which is why GitHub reports NOASSERTION; README declares 'Apache 2.0'. Catalog precedent for restricted-access biosecurity benchmarks is paper-only (asa-abc-bench). Under the task rule, paper-only/unreleased systems are HOLD unless significant; this is a v1 company preprint (LatchBio/Aclid) with no peer review or documented external use found, so HOLD. If the maintainer overrides, use access 'paper-only' (or 'lab-gated' for partner access), never 'open-data' or 'open-source'.

category.note: benchmark is correct (B-only category); consistent with BixBench, BixBench3, scBench-Long.

urls.note: All three proposed record URLs return HTTP 200: https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.19262, https://github.com/latchbio/biosecbench-surveillance, https://github.com/latchbio/biosecbench-surveillance/blob/main/LICENSE. They support their labels, but the GitHub link supports only a prompt-and-metadata subset, not a data release. Note the proposal's sources list GitHub's licence endpoint as reporting NOASSERTION, which is accurate.

text.note: (1) 'partial data release' overstates: no input data, graders, ground truth or trajectories are public; only seven prompts with metadata and aggregate results. (2) 'confident wrong answers and provider refusals of legitimate surveillance work as the two main failure modes' comes from the README, not the paper; the paper scores refusals as a separate third outcome and attributes errors to choices around correct tools (references, thresholds, normalization) and to interpretation, worst in anomaly detection (20%) and genetic-engineering characterization (35%). (3) Pass-rate range 14-50% across sixteen configurations is correct (paper: approximately 14% to 50%, mean 41%). (4) Notes omit that the full set is restricted to qualified partners for biosecurity reasons and that no trajectories are released. (5) Rationale error: the paper does cite the repository. Inputs/outputs/domain text is accurate. Fallback notes if the maintainer adds it as paper-only: 'LatchBio benchmark with Aclid: 100 evaluations in seven task categories, from taxonomic classification to genetic-engineering and anomaly detection, on real or simulated short- and long-read data. Across sixteen model-harness configurations endpoint pass rates ran from about 14% to 50%, with refusals scored separately. For biosecurity reasons the full set, input data, graders and ground truth go only to qualified partners; the public repository holds seven task prompts with metadata and aggregate results. Sibling of BioSecBench-Refusal (arXiv 2607.05462).'

The repo metadata gives license null, GET /repos/latchbio/metagenomicsbench/license returns 404, GET /contents/LICENSE returns 404, and the web blob URL returned 503 twice. The README says 'Apache 2.0 - see [LICENSE](LICENSE)' but the file is absent. The git tree (recursive) holds only README.md (469 B) and 4 eval JSONs (1,950-2,583 B). Each eval JSON contains a task prompt, grader config with ground truth, metadata and a latch:// data_node reference. There is no source code at all, so 'source-available' (public code without an open licence) mislabels the release. The README's 'prompt/vocabulary files, and agent trajectory examples' do not exist in the repo. The paper says these 'will be made available' (future tense, p.12 lines 372-374). Input data are latch:// platform node IDs. Whether those nodes can be reached publicly is UNVERIFIED; the same pattern occurs in the accepted scBench-Long repo, so this point is not decisive on its own. The decisive contrast with the scBench-Long precedent (open-data) is that its repo contains an Apache-2.0 LICENSE text (9,073 B), vocabulary.json files, a manifest and per-model trajectory.json files. metagenomicsbench has none of these. Under MAINTENANCE.md ('Prefer HOLD ... over padding the index with ... unlicensed, unreleased ... entries') and the task default (HOLD when artifact or licence cannot be confirmed), this should be HOLD.

text.note: (1) False content claim: the notes say the repository 'contains four evaluations with prompt and vocabulary files plus example trajectories'. It contains only four eval JSONs; there are no vocabulary files and no trajectories. The proposer appears to have repeated the README, which looks templated from scbench-long. (2) Unreconciled figures: the abstract says 10,200 trajectories from 34 configurations and 60.0%. The Introduction (p.2 line 55) says 9,900 trajectories from 33 model-harness pairs. Methods 6.3 (p.12 line 355) says 9,900 runs. The Discussion (p.9 line 267) says 60.1%. The notes copy the abstract figures only. (3) 'Published metagenomic datasets' as inputs overstates it. Methods 6.1 says the inputs were derived from public datasets, anonymized, and sometimes preprocessed internally into intermediate files (e.g. per-sample ARG detection tables). (4) 'The bioRxiv page served abstract-level content only' is outdated: the full-text PDF is retrievable. (5) The preprint reads as a rushed draft: truncated captions ('Breakdown of awarene'), typos, a truncated DOI in the references, and a Figure 2 caption describing 'long-horizon rates ... 8 independent trials' in a short-horizon benchmark. This is noted for whoever reconsiders it; it is not grounds for rejection.

scope.note: In scope. Hierarchical multi-agent system (planning + supervisor agents coordinating research, prediction, data and report sub-agents) that builds knowledge graphs from live APIs, runs ADMET models, executes generated Python on assay data and writes reports across three case studies (AML candidate generation, retrospective COVID-19 screen reanalysis, MSD prioritisation of ~5000 compounds). autonomy.note: A3 is supported and not inflated. Closure is in silico only: plan execution is gated by human approval and runs 'autonomously under human supervision'; the COVID-19 study is a retrospective reanalysis of a completed dataset; AML candidates are experimentally untested. No physical or wet-lab loop, so A5 is excluded; the approval gate and multi-turn human steering argue against A4. Human gate is disclosed in the proposed notes.

access.note: No licence anywhere. GitHub API license field is null for both repos; /license returns 404 for both; a full recursive tree scan (380 files in repuragent, 1047 in repuragent-web, default branch main) found no LICENSE/COPYING/NOTICE file; no GitHub releases. The paper abstract nonetheless says 'RepurAgent is open source', an author claim that is not backed by a licence, so open-source is excluded. The proposal's source-available label is the right class IF the system were added, but the September 2026 precedent held every comparable lead with the identical rationale 'Author-endorsed repository is public, but no usable license text was confirmed. Hold pending a licensed release' (SciLENS, AgentFold, AutoKD, AutoSR, SAEScientist-Bench, Eureka), and none of the 21 September ADDs lacked a confirmed licence. The hosted instance (repuragent.serve.scilifelab.se, a Gradio app with Log in/Register) requires an account that the README says is manually verified and approved. Root may weigh this author-operated deployment against the August MechAInistic 'platform' precedent; by default, consistency with the September precedent means HOLD.

text.note: Four corrections needed if the record is ever added. (1) Domain and rationale say the system 'designs' experiments or assays. The paper frames experiment design as part of the repurposing lifecycle, but what it demonstrates is 'experimental recommendations' inside a retrospective reanalysis. Suggested domain: 'Drug repurposing across candidate generation, assay-data analysis and candidate prioritisation'. (2) Notes say the authors state 'candidates remain experimentally untested'. This overgeneralises: the paper says the AML candidates are untested, the COVID-19 study is retrospective, and one MSD high-confidence compound was flagged by external experts based on their own unpublished experimental findings and cannot be disclosed for IP reasons. (3) Notes attribute the system to 'Uppsala University, Karolinska Institutet and Pixl Bio'. That list is incomplete: authors also come from Fraunhofer ITMP and FIMM/University of Helsinki. Better: 'Led by Uppsala University's Pharmaceutical Bioinformatics group (pharmbio) with REMEDi4ALL partners'; the paper's COI states J.C.P. and O.S. own shares in Pixl Bio AB. (4) Add that the local app needs an OpenAI API key (README prerequisites) and that the abstract's 'open source' claim lacks a licence.

The paper's Data and Code Availability statement names github.com/HSZD-Team/PerturbTrace, so the repo is author-endorsed.
